text: the ASME Code has only approved six materials for nuclear construction at elevated temperatures, underscoring the need for a more efficient material qualification process. The traditional approach, which relies on extensive testing and modeling, can be lengthy and resource-intensive, requiring a large dataset for designers and engineers to reference during the design and selection process. The Additive Manufacturing Maturation and Transition (AMMT) program aimed to integrate the development of advanced materials and manufacturing techniques, tailored to specific application requirements, design constraints, and functional properties. This approach enables a rapid evaluation pathway for qualification and insertion of new materials. In FY23, LANL conducted baseline characterization of AM 316H stainless steel specimens. Building on this foundation, LANL expanded the dataset in FY24 through a comprehensive investigation. This included destructive testing to further understand the material's behavior, non-destructive testing to evaluate the material's integrity, and the development of a machine- agnostic process parameter framework to ensure consistency across different fabrication platforms. Additionally, LANL created a comprehensive machine maintenance plan to ensure the reliability and performance of AM machines and collected in-situ imaging data during the fabrication process to gain insights into material behavior. The team also explored various post- processing methods to enhance material properties and developed ML models to predict material behavior and properties based on process parameters and material characteristics. The data collection, analysis, archiving, and reporting of these results from all participating sites have been completed for FY24. The LANL results and conclusions are presented in the following sections of this report. UNCLASSIFIED AMMT – 316H SS Los Alamos National Laboratory Page v Machine Agnostics and Machine Maintenance Plan Establishing a machine-agnostic process parameter and machine maintenance plan is crucial for achieving manufacturing readiness for AM parts and paving the way for rapid qualification and certification. However, the qualification process itself is intricate and time-consuming, necessitating meticulous analyses, measurements, and assessments throughout the entire fabrication process, as well as post-acceptance testing. The complexity arises from the numerous variables influencing the AM process, including the type of AM system, system health, material properties, part design, part location, and operator expertise. Currently, there is no single, unified standard that captures the qualification procedures for metal AM, due to the diverse requirements and nuances of different AM systems. Instead, standard organizations have collaborated to develop parallel yet distinct standards for AM metals, as evident in literature, the AMMT 316H work packages, and previous LANL research. To address this challenge, a machine-agnostic process parameter plan can be distilled into four key steps, initiated by the specific application and customer request, as illustrated in Figure 1. This structured approach can help navigate the complex qualification process, ensuring the reliability and performance of AM parts and systems. Figure 1: Machine agnostics process plan. The first step in the machine-agnostic process parameter and machine maintenance plan focuses on the critical triumvirate of design, feedstock, and equipment. To ensure the integrity of the additive manufacturing process, the required feedstock must meet stringent material specifications outlined by engineers, accompanied by vendor certification and rigorous material testing to verify compliance.
